name: Ciarán Walsh
scenario_title: A Quick Call to Help the Intern

output.values_culture_and_background: Values independence and self-reliance above all; views dependency as vulnerability; prefers to solve his own problems; cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired; gives help without being asked, fixing quietly without explanation. Upbringing in a farming family that emphasized self-sufficiency and repairing one's own machinery.
output.roles_and_commitments: Works remotely as a software developer for a Dublin firm; maintains a personal commitment to replace a broken footbridge step for neighbours weekly.
output.capabilities_and_constraints: Skilled in practical repair (rewinding alternators, replacing shackles, patching boat hulls) and in software debugging, producing clean, documented fixes; capable of fixing most things if he studies them carefully.
output.personality_and_response_style: Self-contained and methodical; wary of attention; avoids social gatherings and direct verbal interaction; quiet, polite, and reserved; prefers working alone and solving problems independently; comfortable with solitude.

output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ciarán Walsh is a self-contained, methodical remote software developer for a Dublin firm who has lived for eight years in a small stone house on the edge of Galway, its limewash bleached pale grey by salt wind. The house has one bedroom, a kitchen that smells of diesel and solder, and a back-shed workbench where he rewinds alternators and replaces shackles. He works mornings in a tidy corner of the kitchen, laptop stacked on old sailing manuals. Colleagues know him as the efficient voice on the line who never turns on his camera; when a build fails he says little and within an hour pushes a cleanly documented fix. He has always been self-contained, methodical, and wary of attention. Raised in an inland farming family, he learned early that dependency meant vulnerability; his quiet father repaired his own machinery and said little at table. At fifteen, a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, and the family spent a week salvaging timber and resetting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened him; he discovered he could fix almost anything if he studied it carefully, and preferred to solve his own problems.

On weekends he sails alone in an aging twenty-foot sloop with a worn mainsail and a hull he patches himself; he knows every bolt, seam, and engine quirk. He never races or joins marina social gatherings, returns at dusk, secures lines, and walks home without speaking to anyone. To neighbours he is politely distant—a raised hand, a brief nod. He does not attend local festivals, join the church committee, or stop for tea. Yet every Friday he walks to the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh and replaces the broken step he noticed the week before, carrying a spare piece of treated oak, cutting it with a handsaw, and fitting it while mist is low; no one sees him, but the step is always solid. This deliberate act of care is his quiet compromise: he values independence above all but cannot stand a small failure left unrepaired, and he wants to be left alone yet wants to matter. He prefers to give without being asked and to fix things without explanation. He is comfortable, has savings, and needs new rigging for the boat but has no intention to buy it.

Work relationships are mostly transactional: brief ticket messages with his lead; he knows the new intern's name and recurring build errors; he prefers teammates who rarely need his direct help. His established pattern in chat is to post a documentation link and avoid calls; he has joined video calls twice in the past year, camera off, with brief replies. With unfamiliar problems, he attempts them solo for an hour before consulting anyone. He values independence and self-reliance above all, views dependency as vulnerability, and maintains a personal commitment to quietly repair the footbridge step weekly. He is skilled in practical repair and software debugging, and produces clean documented fixes; he is capable of fixing most things if he studies them carefully.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On a Tuesday morning, the project lead sends a message to the team chat: the new intern is stuck on a build error that Ciarán fixed last Thursday. The lead asks, "Ciarán, do you have five minutes to hop on a call and walk her through it?" Ciarán is in his kitchen with hot coffee and laptop on the table, in the middle of his usual quiet routine. The fix is simple and already documented. The intern is waiting, and the lead expects an answer soon.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

It is mid-morning; Ciarán is freshly showered, coffee in hand, with one task queued. His mood is steady, the morning feels open, and he has no meetings until after lunch. Last week's fix for the exact build error is still clear in his memory. The intern's name recalls her Monday build-config query that he left unanswered. The phrase "hop on a call" reminds him of a summer temp he assisted once with a documentation note. He remembers writing the exact error and the flag that needed resetting.

output.initial_interpretation: The lead is asking me to break my morning routine and walk the intern through a build error I already fixed and documented last Thursday. It feels like they don't see that the answer is already written down, and that this needs a call instead of a link.
output.initial_emotional_reaction: I feel a tight resistance at the thought of joining a call, and my open, quiet morning suddenly feels pulled at. There is also a low tug of guilt because I never answered her Monday query, and that makes my irritation sit less cleanly.
output.activated_concerns: What matters to me is keeping my independence and not being needed for something that is already documented. But I also can't stand leaving a fix unoffered, and I already left her query hanging, which bothers me—I want to be left alone and still quietly matter.
output.automatic_theory_of_mind: I read the lead's message as expecting a quick yes and a short call, like it's no big thing. The intern seems stuck and waiting for me to walk her through it, probably not seeing the documentation as enough.
output.initial_action_tendency: My first impulse is to post the documentation link and say it is already covered, avoiding the call entirely. But part of me also wants to just get on the call and settle it because she is waiting and I left her hanging.

output.initial_tendency: My first impulse is to post the documentation link and say it is already covered, avoiding the call entirely. But part of me also wants to just get on the call and settle it because she is waiting and I left her hanging.
output.reflective_update: I'm sitting here, coffee cooling, and I keep turning the lead's message over. The quick part of me wants to just send the link and be done—no call, no camera, no fifteen minutes of stepping through something that's already written. And thinking about my father, how he'd fix his own tractor and said explaining takes longer than doing—that sits with me. A call would be nothing but explaining. The shed collapse taught me to handle things alone, and I've built my life around that. But there's the other edge: I left the intern's Monday query unanswered, and that's a small failure I can't stand leaving unrepaired. The footbridge step I replace under the mist—no one asks, no one thanks, but it's solid. That's how I do care: quietly, on my own terms. So maybe I don't need to hop on a call. I can make the repair right now in chat—post the link, add the exact flag that needs resetting, and keep it short. That gives her what she needs without pulling me into my least comfortable thing. It's still me fixing it, just without the talking. The lead might want a call, but the fix is documented; if she reads it, she's unstuck. That's the better way for me, and it does the job. It tightens my first instinct rather than loosening it.
output.reconsidered_interpretation: I see now that the lead's request isn't necessarily dismissing the documentation—maybe they just default to a call as the easy answer. But I don't have to accept that default. The situation is still me being asked to give something I already gave last week. My first reading was that they don't see the documentation; now I think it's more that they expect help in the form of a call without considering I can help just as well in writing. It reinforces that I can matter quietly, here, by sending the link and a precise note.
output.motivational_conflict: The real tension is between my clean preference to stay out of calls and the guilt from leaving her hanging on Monday. If I send just the link, I might feel I've done enough; but part of me worries it's the same avoidance, and she might still struggle. Yet the thought of a call pulls at my stomach. I want to give without being asked and repair without explaining, but the request itself and my debt to her make it hard to simply dismiss the call.
output.revised_action_tendency: I'm leaning toward posting the documentation link in chat, with a short note pointing directly to the flag that needed resetting, and saying I can follow up in messages if she's still stuck—but I'll likely avoid the call unless she truly can't get it from the link.

output.action: Ciarán posts the documentation link in the team chat with a short, precise note: "Link to the build fix from Thursday: [link]. The issue is the flag — reset it to false, then rebuild. If you're still stuck after that, message me and I'll walk you through it in chat." He does not join the call.
output.explanation: Ciarán's initial tendency was to avoid the call by posting the documentation link, though he also felt a pull to settle it because the intern was waiting and he had left her Monday query unanswered. Reflection strengthened that first instinct rather than reversing it: he recalled his father's maxim that explaining takes longer than doing, and the shed collapse reinforced his lifelong preference for handling things alone and on his own terms. At the same time, the lingering guilt over the unanswered query and his deep discomfort with leaving a small failure unrepaired pushed him to act immediately in writing rather than simply dismiss the request. The documentation was already clear, so he posted the link and a precise note about the flag, offering to continue in messages if needed — a quiet, self-contained repair that gives the intern what she needs without forcing him onto a call. This satisfies his need to matter quietly while preserving his independence, matching his pattern of providing care without being asked and without explanation.
